title: remove lazyeval implementations for dplyr verbs
description:
We're trying to remove the `*_()` verbs from `dplyr` : 

https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5573
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/5592

Initially we'd just like to remove the fallbacks that call the underscore function, and then later we'll remove the underscore function altogether. 

For example, we'd like to remove this:  

```r
group_by.default <- function(.data, ..., add = FALSE, .drop = group_by_drop_default(.data)) {		
   group_by_(.data, .dots = compat_as_lazy_dots(...), add = add)		
 }
```

but ggvis uses them, e.g.: https://github.com/rstudio/ggvis/blob/master/R/dplyr.R

```r
group_by_.ggvis <- function(.data, ..., .dots, add = FALSE) {
  dots <- lazyeval::all_dots(.dots, ...)
  pieces <- extract_lazy_inputs(dots)

  register_computation(.data, pieces$inputs, "group_by", function(data, args) {
    dplyr::group_by_(data, .dots = lapply(pieces$lazy, add_args, args),
      add = add)
  })
}
```

Perhaps `ggvis` could instead define methods for the non underscore verbs instead ?

title: ggvis objects as relational databases
description:
So, theoretically, every data structure should be able to be expressed as a relational database. The ggvis object list structure is pretty confusing, and I was thinking a relational model might help. Here's a quick demonstration

``` r

library(ggvis)
library(dplyr)

# functions to recursively remove nulls, just to make things easier on me
is.NullOb <- function(x) if(!(is.function(x))) is.null(x) | all(sapply(x, is.null)) else FALSE
rmNullObs <- function(x) {
  if(!(is.function(x))) {
    x = x[!(sapply(x, is.NullOb))]
    lapply(x, function(x) if (is.list(x)) rmNullObs(x) else x)
  }
}

# data frames don't seem to play well with symbol columns? 
# need to make sure list variables (like value) have 1 symbol per item for tidy reasons
as_data_frame_fix = function(x) {
  x = x %>% 
    lapply(function(x) if (!(is.vector(x))) list(x) else(x)) %>%
    as_data_frame

  if("value" %in% names(x))
    x %>%
    mutate(value = 
             ifelse(!is.list(value),
                    list(value),
                    value)) else x }

prefix = function(df, prefix) {
  names(df) = paste(prefix, names(df) , sep = ".")
  df
}

object =
  iris %>%
  ggvis(
    ~Sepal.Length,
    ~Sepal.Width,
    fill = ~Species,
    stroke = ~Petal.Width
  ) %>%
  layer_points() %>%
  # obviously, because of the recursive removing of nulls, this framework is incomplete
  # as.data.frame fails with nulls, NA's should be used in the database version
  rmNullObs

database = list()

# marks only has one entry in this case ?
database$mark = data_frame(
  mark.type = object$marks[[1]]$type,
  mark.data = list(object$marks[[1]]$data),
  mark.ID = 1,
  object.ID = 1)

# object$props seems to be two replicates of object$marks[[1]]$props, minus the size property
database$property =
  object$marks[[1]]$props %>%
  lapply(as_data_frame_fix) %>%
  bind_rows %>%
  prefix("property") %>%
  rename(property.name = property.property) %>%
  mutate(object.ID = 1)

database$object = data_frame(
  object.ID = 1,
  object.data = object$data)

# in this case, scale might be able to fit into property with missing values for the size property
# kept them separate because I assume size will never have a scale
database$scale = 
  object$scales %>%
  lapply(as_data_frame_fix) %>%
  bind_rows %>%
  # both in already in database$property. databases hate duplication
  select(-name, -label) %>%
  prefix("scale") %>%
  rename(property.name = scale.property) %>%
  mutate(object.ID = 1)
```

Some notes:
I almost always prefix column names with the unit of analysis. It makes natural joins much safer
I typically denote join tables (or really, intersecting unit of analysis tables) with the 2 units of analysis separated by double underscores. I don't see any required here
I like to avoid pluralized names
Relational databases instead of list structures (I think) is much more broadly applicable
Because of the object ID, such a database can hold one or many ggvis objects

layer_bars does not work if `x` and `y` are not initially specified in `ggvis` call
description:
The following does not work:
```
library(magrittr)
library(ggvis)

mtcars %>%
ggvis() %>%
group_by(gear) %>%
layer_bars(
    x = ~factor(cyl),
    y = ~mpg,
    fill = ~factor(gear),
    width = 1
) %>% 
scale_ordinal('x')
```
Error is: `Error in UseMethod("prop_label") : no applicable method for 'prop_label' applied to an object of class "NULL"`

But the following does:
```
library(magrittr)
library(ggvis)

mtcars %>%
ggvis( #specifying the x and y here now, instead of later
    x = ~factor(cyl),
    y = ~mpg
) %>%
group_by(gear) %>%
layer_bars(
    fill = ~factor(gear),
    width = 1
) %>% 
scale_ordinal('x')
```
Even the following works:
```
library(magrittr)
library(ggvis)

mtcars %>%
ggvis(
    x = ~hp,
    y = ~mpg
) %>%
group_by(gear) %>%
layer_bars(
    x = ~factor(cyl),
    y = ~mpg,
    fill = ~factor(gear),
    width = 1
) %>% 
scale_ordinal('x')```
```
i.e. `layer_bars` works only if `x` and `y` are initially set in the initial `ggvis` call.

The source code for `layer_bars` seems to ask for `'x.update'`, which I'm guessing only works if `x` is initially defined.

This does not seem to be the case for `layer_points`, i.e.
```
library(magrittr)
library(ggvis)

mtcars %>%
ggvis() %>%
layer_points(
    x = ~factor(gear),
    y = ~mpg
) %>% 
scale_ordinal('x')
```
works fine.

In my opinion, this should be made consistent... if some marks allow for empty initial values for props, I think all of them should?

Also: thank you, to the entire team, for making such a great contribution to the data community. I know this isn't high on your priority list right now, but there are definitely people out there who love `ggvis` and are hoping for further development.

title: Non-reactive version of add_tooltip() to remove the restrictive shiny dependency
description:
Currently, `add_tooltip(vis, html, on)` requires a function for the `html` argument that returns the html to render in the tooltip. Since, the tooltip relies on a function, reactivity is required and _ggvis_ switches interactive mode which requires _shiny_. Unfortunately, _shiny_ visualizations have much greater overhead and demand expensive software or services to share at scale.

I propose a version of `add_tooltip()` where `html` accepts a column from the input data.frame (`vis`). The user would precompute the tooltip html and store it as a character column in the data.frame. _ggvis_ualizations based on non-reactive tooltips should be exportable to html documents and therefore easily distributed, embedded, and freed from the shackles of _shiny_.

In many cases, individual observation identification is the single most important reason for interactivity.

title: treefacet question w/ possible fix for export
description:
tl;dr - treefacet isn't known to vega and use of facet seems to work just fine with the ggvis tests and a cookbook visual check. Granted these are simplistic so is there a reason treefacet is being used rather than the known facet?

---

 The other day I ran into an issue with export_png failing when browser viewing worked just fine; it turned out to be the use of `label` instead of `labels` within my axis props. A waste of a time trying to run that down with vg2png's unhelpful 'unknown' but it told me that there is some possible argument matching being done that doesn't get done with export.

That got me to thinking about the reported issue with export_png and grouped data reported in [this long ggvis group post](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/ggvis/export_png/ggvis/eQ4XHmRnCCc/G7hwcR4vvh4J) and on [this SO question](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/27674431/exporting-ggvis-plot-with-grouped-data) and in ggvis issue https://github.com/rstudio/ggvis/issues/332.

A little checking resulted in the realization that while `treefacet` works fine when `ggvis.js` is available it is just plainly **not** list in vega's [data manipulation transforms](https://github.com/trifacta/vega/wiki/Data-Transforms#data-manipulation-transforms). After making a [branch that alters the instances of `treefacet` to `facet`](https://github.com/Thell/ggvis/tree/thell/fix-export-of-group-transformed) and testing that the ggvis package works as well as the `export_png` I'm left wondering if there is a reason for that name choice that isn't apparent.

title: layer_segment
description:
It would be handy to have a layer_segment().  At the moment you can get the functionality by reshaping data and feeding a grouped version to layer_paths.  I've written a function to do this below, but turning this into a full blown layer_segment() is beyond me, so hopefully someone else can take it on at some time.

``` R
library(dplyr)
library(ggvis)
rearrange_segments <- function(segs){
   # segs must have columns x, y, x2 and y2.  TODO - make that more flexible.
   # The output has columns for x, y and group and is grouped ready for use by layer_paths().
   # TODO - turn this into a proper layer_segment()

   # Identify the secondary columns for later use
   other_cols <- segs %>%
      select(-x, -y, -x2, -y2)

   # reshape the four columns that we need to be in longer shape
   # First we break up into two rectangles with the same variable names
   segs1 <- segs %>% select(x, y)
   segs2 <-  segs %>% 
      select(x2, y2) %>%
      rename(x=x2, y=y2)

   # Then we join them back together, alternating rows
   n <- nrow(segs1) * 2
   both  <- data.frame(x=numeric(n), y=numeric(n))
   both[seq(from=1, to = n-1, by = 2), ] <- segs1
   both[seq(from=2, to = n, by = 2), ] <- segs2

   # Add back in the other columns other than x, y, etc if there are any.
   # There's probably a more elegant way to do this than one at a time in a loop.
   if(ncol(other_cols) > 0){
      for(i in 1:ncol(other_cols)){
         both[seq(from=1, to = n-1, by = 2), names(other_cols)[i]] <- other_cols[ ,i]
         both[seq(from=2, to = n, by = 2), names(other_cols)[i]] <- other_cols[ , i]
      }
   }

   both$group <- rep(1:(n / 2), each=2)
   return(both %>% group_by(group))
}



# Example.  Note rearrange_segments needs variables x, y, x2, y2.
set.seed(123)
n <- 15
df <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n), y=rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), y2 = rnorm(n), 
                 name=letters[1:n], unnecessary=letters[n:1])

df %>%
   rearrange_segments() %>%
   ggvis() %>%
   layer_paths(x = ~x, y = ~y, stroke = ~name)
```

title: compute_bin() - zero-row - using group_by()
description:
As I understand the ggvis "social contract", zero-row data frames are allowed, if the data frame has all the needed variables.

Using `compute_bin()` on ungrouped, empty data-frames, we still get a data frame with variables:

``` R
mtcars %>%
  filter(mpg > 100) %>%
  compute_bin(x_var = ~mpg) 
```

Using `compute_bin()` for grouped, empty, data-frames, we do not get any variables:

``` R
mtcars %>%
  filter(mpg > 100) %>%
  group_by(fcyl = factor(cyl)) %>%
  compute_bin(x_var = ~mpg)  
```

As a result, this works:

``` R
mtcars %>%
  filter(mpg > 100) %>%
  ggvis(x = ~mpg) %>%
  layer_histograms()  
```

This doesn't:

``` R
mtcars %>%
  filter(mpg > 100) %>%
  group_by(fcyl = factor(cyl)) %>%
  ggvis(x = ~mpg) %>%
  layer_histograms()  
```

title: Interactive plots with slider controls start with wrong vertical padding in RStudio viewer
description:
When running this in RStudio, there's too much space at the bottom:

```
qvis(mtcars, ~wt, binwidth = input_slider(0, 2, value = 1, step = 0.1))
```

Resizing it makes it reset to the correct amount of space at the bottom.

It's because `resizeToWindow()` calculates the amount of extra vertical space after the HTML for the slider is emitted to the page, but before the slider is initialized. At that point, it's not actually a slider, but a few rows of text, which takes more vertical space.

Probably the solution is to run `resizeToWindow()` after the slider is initialized.

title: transformation of datetime from s to ms
description:
I understand if this is not easily solved, but it does present a couple of gotchas.

In R, time is measured in seconds from the origin, 1970-01-01 UTC. 

In the Javascript implementation, time is measured in milliseconds. 

ggvis makes the conversion automatically, whenever a datetime is involved.

The problem is in those cases where ggvis feeds back those datetimes to the user, or to the R program.

A couple of use cases:
1. Tooltips display datetimes as numbers representing the milliseconds from the origin.
2. Using datetimes as "key" will not allow you to match your selected data to your original data.

If these are not easy things to fix programatically, perhaps the user can be alerted to workarounds.

I would not want to suggest a workaround where users divide their fed-back datetimes by 1000, as that might reintroduce bugs if/when there is a fix on the ggvis end.

Instead, my first thought is to suggest using an integer key, and then to use the datetimes from the original dataframe, not from the feedback from ggvis.

Reproducible example as a gist and a shiny app:

https://gist.github.com/ijlyttle/6fd7d4697812f96c7eb0

https://ijlyttle.shinyapps.io/ggvis_dtm_gotcha/ggvis_dtm_gotcha.Rmd

title: ggvis within shiny app vs. subApp
description:
Within shiny, ggvis renders differently depending on if shiny renders it in an app or in a subApp.

By app, I mean running shiny app in the traditional way, i.e. from the command line.

By subApp, I mean as a part of an rmarkdown document run from shiny.
### (somewhat) short version
#### navbarPage

Within a shiny app navbarPage, ggvis does not conform to the horizontal dimension of the column in which it is placed. However, each tab is generally legible.

Within a shiny subApp navbarPage, using multiple fluidRows, any ggvis that is not on the tab displayed initially gets distorted.
#### fluidPage

Within a shiny app fluidPage, using multiple fluidRows, ggvis does not conform to the horizontal dimension of the column in which it is placed. However, each ggvis is generally legible.

Within a shiny subApp fluidPage, using multiple fluidRows, ggvis does conform to the horizontal dimension of the column, but a ggvis in the second row is distorted.
### longer version

https://gist.github.com/ijlyttle/a37bea7952f1ac9f12ba

For what it's worth, within a shiny app each ggvis has its own gear icon in the upper right of each plot. Within a sub app, there appears a single gear icon in the upper right of the subApp.
### Thoughts on ggvis placement within shiny apps (and subApps)

This may not be the place, but I wonder if ggvis could have an option within `set_options` such as `elastic_horizontal = TRUE` (I'm sure there's a better name). In this case, ggvis would resize itself to occupy all the horizontal space available to it. The vertical dimension would either be the `height`, or, if `keep_aspect == TRUE`, the height according to the original aspect ratio and the (available) width. 

Happy to split this up into separate issues, if that's the right thing to do.

Options for more streamlined DSL for props()
description:
These are some of the possibilities for the DSL for specifying within the `props()` function. This function has the approximately the same purpose as the `aes()` function in ggplot2.

A property is either scaled or unscaled. Examples of scaled values are: numeric value mapped to x position, and a categorical variable mapped to colors. Examples of unscaled values are: specifying a constant color for points, like "red", or a column in a data set that contains raw color names, like "#000000", "#ffffff", "red", etc.

The value should also be an expression to be evaluated at render time, a constant value, or a (reactive) input object.

Here are there are six different combinations and some examples of their use:
1. Scaled expression: Mapping a variable to a property. Similar to `aes(x = wt)` in ggplot2.
2. Scaled constant: Used for setting the x or y position of a line/point.
3. Scaled reactive: For interactive input - perhaps for adding lines at particular x/y values?
4. Unscaled expression: An expression, which, when evaluated in the data set, returns a vector of raw values, like `c("red", "red", "black")`.
5. Unscaled constant: A raw value like `"red"`.
6. Unscaled reactive: Interactive inputs setting color/size/opacity of points.

1 and 5 will probably be the most common use cases.

The options shown below are a subset of a long list of alternatives.
### Option 1.5
- scaled expr: `x ~ quote(mpg)`
- scaled cnst: `x ~ 1`
- scaled rctv: `x ~ input_slider()`
- unscld expr: `fill = quote(col)`
- unscld cnst: `fill = "red"`
- unscld rctv: `fill = input_slider()`
- prop obj   : `y = prop(...)`

Cons: most common operation is longest (~ + quote).
### Option 3
- scaled expr: `x ~ mpg`
- scaled cnst: `x ~ 1`
- scaled rctv: `x ~ input_slider()`
- unscld expr: `fill ~ I(col)`
- unscld cnst: `fill ~ I("red")`
- unscld rctv: `fill ~ I(input_slider())`
- prop obj   : `y = prop(...)`

Cons:
### Option 4
- scaled expr: `x ~ mpg`
- scaled cnst: `x ~ 1`
- scaled rctv: `y = input_slider()`
- unscld expr: `fill ~ I(col)`
- unscld cnst: `fill = "red"`, or `fill = I("red")`
- unscld rctv: `fill = I(input_slider())`
- prop obj   : `y = prop(...)`

Pros: No non-standard evaluation, Hadley can implement easily 
Cons: lack of symmetry, confusing
### Option 5

By default, expressions are evaluated
`~` means to not evaluate the expression

`=`  means to use scale = TRUE
`:=` means to use scale = FALSE
- scaled expr: `x = ~mpg`
- scaled cnst: `x = 1`
- scaled rctv: `x = input_slider()`
- unscld expr: `fill := ~col`
- unscld cnst: `fill := "red"`
- unscld rctv: `fill := input_slider()`
- prop obj   : `y = prop(...)`
### Option 9

`~` means to not evaluate the expression. Also default to scale=TRUE.
`=` means to evaluate the expression. Also default to scale=FALSE.

scaled() means to force the object to have scale=TRUE
unscaled() means to force the object to have scaled=FALSE
- scaled expr: `x ~ mpg`
- scaled cnst: `x = scaled(1)`
- scaled rctv: `x = scaled(input_slider())`
- unscld expr: `fill ~ unscaled(col)`
- unscld cnst: `fill = "red"`
- unscld rctv: `fill = input_slider()`
- prop obj   : `y = prop(...)`
### Option 10

By default, expressions are evaluated
`~` means to not evaluate the expression

Default is to use scale=TRUE
`I()` means to use scale=FALSE
- scaled expr: `x = ~mpg`
- scaled cnst: `x = 1`
- scaled rctv: `x = input_slider()`
- unscld expr: `fill = ~I(col)`
- unscld cnst: `fill = I("red")`
- unscld rctv: `fill = I(input_slider())`
- prop obj   : `y = prop(...)`
